text:
A vaccine lets the immune system practice fighting an infection without the risk of the disease itself.

The vaccine supplies fragments of the pathogen, called antigens. They may come from inactivated virions, from purified protein subunits, or from mRNA that deltoid muscle cells translate into protein. The fragments drain to lymph nodes. There, dendritic cells pick up the antigens and display their peptides on MHC molecules.

Billions of helper T cell receptor variants are generated at random, and the cells whose receptors match the epitope are selected. These helper T cells then activate B cells, which multiply inside germinal centers. In these sites, somatic hypermutation improves antibody binding over two to four weeks.

Most effector cells then die. Long-lived plasma cells and reserves of memory lymphocytes persist for years, sometimes decades.

Immunologists know the payoff comes later. On real exposure, a secondary response starts within days, instead of the week or more the primary response takes. It often neutralizes the pathogen before symptoms appear.

Aluminum-salt adjuvants, used since the 1930s, strengthen the alarm signal. Boosters repeat the training, and immunity grows stronger.
